::: {.callout-note .objectives}
## Learning objectives

By the end of this lesson you will be able to:

- use the four functions `d*()`, `p*()`, `q*()` and `r*()` for any distribution in R, and explain what each one returns;
- recognise situations described by the **Bernoulli**, **binomial**, **Poisson**, **uniform** and **normal** distributions, and compute probabilities with them;
- standardise a value (z-score) and use `pnorm()`/`qnorm()` to find probabilities and cut-offs;
- recognise the shapes of the **t**, **chi-square** and **F** distributions used in later tests;
- read a **QQ-plot** and judge whether a normal model is a reasonable description of a variable.
:::

```{r}
#| label: setup
#| include: false
source(here::here("_common.R"))
```

```{r}
#| label: packages
library(ggplot2)
```

## 1. Why do we need distributions?

In the [previous lesson](28-randomness-simulation.qmd) we simulated dice and coins by listing every outcome and its probability. Real questions are often more complex:

- *A student guesses all 20 answers of a multiple-choice quiz. How likely is a pass?*
- *An emergency room receives 3 patients per hour on average. How often will 6 or more arrive in one hour?*
- *How unusual is a Gentoo penguin weighing more than 6 kg?*

Each question is about a random variable, and in each case a **probability distribution** — a mathematical model that says which values are possible and how likely they are — answers it in one line of R. A small set of distributions turns up again and again because they describe common ways in which data are generated: counting successes, counting events, adding up many small effects.

## 2. The `d`/`p`/`q`/`r` family

Every distribution in R comes with four functions. Their names are a **prefix** plus the distribution's short name (`binom`, `pois`, `unif`, `norm`, `t`, `chisq`, `f`, …):

| Prefix | Question it answers | Normal example | Returns |
|---|---|---|---|
| `d` | How likely is *this* value? (height of the curve) | `dnorm(1)` | density (continuous) or probability (discrete) |
| `p` | How likely is a value **≤ x**? | `pnorm(1)` | cumulative probability, between 0 and 1 |
| `q` | Which value has probability `p` below it? | `qnorm(0.9)` | a quantile (the inverse of `p`) |
| `r` | Give me random values | `rnorm(1000)` | simulated data |

```{r}
#| label: dpqr-standard-normal
dnorm(1)        # height of the standard normal curve at x = 1
pnorm(1)        # P(X <= 1)
qnorm(0.9)      # the value with 90% of the distribution below it
set.seed(1)
rnorm(5)        # five random values
```

```{r}
#| label: fig-dpqr
#| fig-cap: "The four functions for the standard normal distribution."
#| fig-subcap:
#|   - "d: the height of the curve at x = 1"
#|   - "p: the area to the left of x = 1"
#|   - "q: the x with 90% of the area to its left"
#|   - "r: random draws (histogram) follow the curve"
#| layout-ncol: 2
grid <- data.frame(x = seq(-4, 4, length.out = 400))
grid$density <- dnorm(grid$x)
base <- ggplot(grid, aes(x, density)) + labs(x = "x", y = "Density")

base + geom_line(linewidth = 1) +
  annotate("segment", x = 1, xend = 1, y = 0, yend = dnorm(1),
           colour = "#D55E00", linewidth = 1) +
  annotate("point", x = 1, y = dnorm(1), colour = "#D55E00", size = 3)

base + geom_area(data = subset(grid, x <= 1), fill = "#56B4E9") +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1)

base + geom_area(data = subset(grid, x <= qnorm(0.9)), fill = "#009E73") +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = qnorm(0.9), colour = "#D55E00", linewidth = 1)

set.seed(1)
ggplot(data.frame(x = rnorm(1000)), aes(x)) +
  geom_histogram(aes(y = after_stat(density)), bins = 30,
                 fill = "grey75", colour = "white") +
  geom_line(data = grid, aes(x, density), linewidth = 1) +
  labs(x = "x", y = "Density")
```

::: {.callout-tip .read-output}
## How to read the four panels

- **(a)** `dnorm(1)` = `r round(dnorm(1), 3)` is a *height*, not a probability. For continuous variables only *areas* are probabilities.
- **(b)** `pnorm(1)` = `r round(pnorm(1), 3)`: the shaded area — about `r round(100 * pnorm(1))`% of values are below 1.
- **(c)** `qnorm(0.9)` = `r round(qnorm(0.9), 3)` goes the other way: from an area (0.9) to a value. `p` and `q` undo each other: `pnorm(qnorm(0.9))` is 0.9.
- **(d)** `rnorm()` produces data whose histogram follows the curve. This is how we simulate.
:::

Two tricks you will use constantly:

- **Upper tail.** $P(X > x) = 1 - P(X \le x)$, so use `1 - pnorm(x)` or, more accurately for tiny probabilities, `pnorm(x, lower.tail = FALSE)`.
- **Intervals.** $P(a < X \le b) =$ `pnorm(b) - pnorm(a)`.

## 3. Bernoulli and binomial: counting successes

A **Bernoulli** trial has two outcomes: success (1) with probability $p$, failure (0) with probability $1-p$. A coin toss, a patient who recovers or not, a customer who buys or not.

The **binomial** distribution counts the **number of successes in $n$ independent Bernoulli trials** with the same $p$. We write $X \sim \text{Binomial}(n, p)$. A Bernoulli variable is simply a binomial with $n = 1$.

*A student guesses all 20 questions of a quiz; each question has 4 options, so $p = 0.25$.* The number of correct answers is $\text{Binomial}(20, 0.25)$.

```{r}
#| label: binom-quiz
dbinom(5, size = 20, prob = 0.25)                     # P(X = 5)
pbinom(7, size = 20, prob = 0.25)                     # P(X <= 7)
pbinom(9, size = 20, prob = 0.25, lower.tail = FALSE) # P(X >= 10)
```

Note the last line: for a discrete variable $P(X \ge 10) = 1 - P(X \le 9)$, so the cut-off is **9**, not 10. Guessing gives a pass mark of 10/20 with probability `r round(pbinom(9, 20, 0.25, lower.tail = FALSE), 3)`: unlikely but not impossible.

```{r}
#| label: fig-binom
#| fig-cap: "Binomial(20, 0.25): probability of each number of correct answers when guessing. The orange bars are 10 or more correct (a pass)."
quiz <- data.frame(correct = 0:20,
                   prob = dbinom(0:20, size = 20, prob = 0.25))
quiz$pass <- quiz$correct >= 10

ggplot(quiz, aes(correct, prob, fill = pass)) +
  geom_col() +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c(`FALSE` = "#0072B2", `TRUE` = "#E69F00")) +
  labs(x = "Number of correct answers", y = "Probability", fill = "Pass")
```

For a discrete distribution the `d` function gives real probabilities (the bar heights), and they sum to 1. Let us check the model against a simulation:

```{r}
#| label: binom-sim
set.seed(28)
guesses <- rbinom(10000, size = 20, prob = 0.25)  # 10,000 simulated students
mean(guesses >= 10)
mean(guesses)                                     # compare with n * p = 5
```

::: {.callout-note .deeper collapse="true"}
## Going deeper: the binomial formula

$$
P(X = k) = \binom{n}{k} p^k (1-p)^{n-k}, \qquad k = 0, 1, \ldots, n,
$$

where $\binom{n}{k}$ = `choose(n, k)` counts the ways of placing $k$ successes among $n$ trials. Check: `choose(20, 5) * 0.25^5 * 0.75^15` equals `dbinom(5, 20, 0.25)`. The mean and variance are $E(X) = np$ and $\operatorname{Var}(X) = np(1-p)$. The binomial assumes a **fixed** number of trials, **independent** trials and the **same** $p$ for every trial.
:::

## 4. Poisson: counting events

The **Poisson** distribution describes the **number of events in a fixed interval** of time or space when events happen independently at a constant average rate $\lambda$ ("lambda"): calls per hour, typos per page, cases of a rare disease per year. Unlike the binomial there is no upper limit on the count.

*An emergency room receives on average 3 patients per hour.*

```{r}
#| label: pois-er
dpois(0, lambda = 3)                     # P(no patients in an hour)
ppois(5, lambda = 3, lower.tail = FALSE) # P(6 or more)
```

```{r}
#| label: fig-pois
#| fig-cap: "Poisson distributions with average rates 1, 3 and 8. As the rate grows the distribution moves right, spreads out and becomes more symmetric."
pois_df <- expand.grid(k = 0:18, lambda = c(1, 3, 8))
pois_df$prob <- dpois(pois_df$k, pois_df$lambda)

ggplot(pois_df, aes(k, prob)) +
  geom_col(fill = "#009E73") +
  facet_wrap(~ lambda, ncol = 3, labeller = label_both) +
  labs(x = "Number of events", y = "Probability")
```

A distinctive property: for a Poisson variable the **mean equals the variance**, both equal to $\lambda$.

```{r}
#| label: pois-mean-var
set.seed(3)
arrivals <- rpois(10000, lambda = 3)
c(mean = mean(arrivals), variance = var(arrivals))
```

Real count data often have a variance *larger* than the mean (*overdispersion*), something we will check in [Poisson regression](../09-regression/42-poisson-regression.qmd).

::: {.callout-note .deeper collapse="true"}
## Going deeper: Poisson as a limit of the binomial

$P(X = k) = e^{-\lambda}\lambda^k / k!$. If $n$ is large and $p$ small, $\text{Binomial}(n, p)$ is almost identical to $\text{Poisson}(\lambda = np)$: many opportunities, each with a tiny chance. Compare `dbinom(0:5, 1000, 0.003)` with `dpois(0:5, 3)`: they agree to about three decimal places.
:::

## 5. Uniform: all values equally likely

The continuous **uniform** distribution on $[a, b]$ gives every value in the interval the same density; its curve is flat. `runif()` (used in the last lesson) draws from it.

*A bus comes every 10 minutes and you arrive at a random time.* Your wait is $\text{Uniform}(0, 10)$.

```{r}
#| label: unif-bus
punif(7, min = 0, max = 10, lower.tail = FALSE)  # P(wait > 7 minutes)
qunif(0.5, min = 0, max = 10)                    # median wait
```

For a uniform the probability of an interval is simply its length divided by $b - a$: a wait longer than 7 minutes has probability $3/10$.

## 6. The normal distribution

The **normal** (or *Gaussian*) distribution is the famous symmetric bell curve. It is described by two numbers: the mean $\mu$ (its centre) and the standard deviation $\sigma$ (its spread). We write $X \sim N(\mu, \sigma)$; in R: `dnorm(x, mean = mu, sd = sigma)`.

Why is it everywhere? Variables that result from **adding up many small, independent effects** (genes, environment, measurement error…) tend to be approximately normal. And, crucially for this course, **averages of samples** are approximately normal even when the data are not — the Central Limit Theorem of the [next lesson](30-sampling-distributions.qmd).

### The 68–95–99.7 rule

Whatever $\mu$ and $\sigma$, the same proportions of a normal distribution lie within 1, 2 and 3 standard deviations of the mean:

```{r}
#| label: rule-689599
k <- 1:3
pnorm(k) - pnorm(-k)
```

```{r}
#| label: fig-689599
#| fig-cap: "The 68–95–99.7 rule: about 68% of values lie within 1 SD of the mean, 95% within 2 SD and 99.7% within 3 SD."
bands <- data.frame(x = seq(-4, 4, length.out = 800))
bands$density <- dnorm(bands$x)
bands$band <- cut(abs(bands$x), breaks = c(0, 1, 2, 3, Inf),
                  labels = c("within 1 SD", "1-2 SD", "2-3 SD", "beyond 3 SD"),
                  include.lowest = TRUE)

ggplot(bands, aes(x, density)) +
  geom_ribbon(aes(ymin = 0, ymax = density, fill = band,
                  group = interaction(band, x > 0))) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = -3:3,
                     labels = c("-3 SD", "-2 SD", "-1 SD", "mean",
                                "+1 SD", "+2 SD", "+3 SD")) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "Density", fill = NULL)
```

### Standardisation and z-scores

To compare a value with a normal distribution we measure how many standard deviations it lies from the mean: the **z-score**

$$
z = \frac{x - \mu}{\sigma}.
$$

If $X \sim N(\mu, \sigma)$, then $Z = (X-\mu)/\sigma \sim N(0, 1)$, the **standard normal**. Any normal probability can therefore be computed on the standard scale — this is exactly what the tables at the back of old statistics books did. In R you can skip the step and pass `mean` and `sd` directly.

### Example: heavy Gentoo penguins

The body mass of Gentoo penguins is roughly symmetric. Let us model it with a normal distribution whose mean and SD are estimated from the data:

```{r}
#| label: gentoo-fit
gentoo <- penguins$body_mass[penguins$species == "Gentoo"]
gentoo <- gentoo[!is.na(gentoo)]
mu    <- mean(gentoo)
sigma <- sd(gentoo)
c(mean = mu, sd = sigma)
```

**Finding a probability.** How likely is a Gentoo heavier than 5,500 g?

```{r}
#| label: gentoo-prob
z <- (5500 - mu) / sigma
z
pnorm(z, lower.tail = FALSE)                          # via the z-score
pnorm(5500, mean = mu, sd = sigma, lower.tail = FALSE) # same, directly
mean(gentoo > 5500)                                    # observed proportion
```

A 5,500 g penguin is `r round(z, 2)` standard deviations above the mean. The model says that about `r round(100 * pnorm(5500, mu, sigma, lower.tail = FALSE))`% of Gentoos are heavier; in our sample the proportion is `r round(100 * mean(gentoo > 5500))`%. A model is a simplification: close agreement is what we hope for, not exact equality.

**Finding a cut-off.** Above which mass are the heaviest 10% of Gentoos? Now we know the probability and want the value, so we use `qnorm()`:

```{r}
#| label: gentoo-cutoff
qnorm(0.90, mean = mu, sd = sigma)                 # model
quantile(gentoo, 0.90)                             # data
qnorm(c(0.025, 0.975), mean = mu, sd = sigma)      # middle 95%
```

```{r}
#| label: fig-gentoo-tail
#| fig-cap: "Normal model for Gentoo body mass. The shaded area is the model's probability of a mass above 5,500 g."
g_grid <- data.frame(
  mass = seq(mu - 4 * sigma, mu + 4 * sigma, length.out = 400)
)
g_grid$density <- dnorm(g_grid$mass, mean = mu, sd = sigma)

ggplot(g_grid, aes(mass, density)) +
  geom_area(data = subset(g_grid, mass >= 5500), fill = "#E69F00") +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 5500, linetype = "dashed") +
  labs(x = "Body mass (g)", y = "Density")
```

::: {.callout-note .deeper collapse="true"}
## Going deeper: the normal density

$$
f(x) = \frac{1}{\sigma\sqrt{2\pi}} \exp\!\left(-\frac{(x-\mu)^2}{2\sigma^2}\right).
$$

$P(a < X \le b) = \int_a^b f(x)\,dx$, which has no closed form; `pnorm()` computes it numerically. The important quantile `qnorm(0.975)` = `r round(qnorm(0.975), 3)` ≈ 1.96 is where the "± 1.96 standard errors" of 95% confidence intervals comes from (see [Confidence intervals](../08-inference/32-confidence-intervals.qmd)).
:::

## 7. Families we will meet in tests: t, chi-square, F

Three more continuous distributions appear as **reference distributions** for test statistics. You do not need their formulas, only their shapes and where they show up. They all have one or two parameters called **degrees of freedom** (df), which depend on the sample size.

```{r}
#| label: fig-t
#| fig-cap: "t distributions with 1, 3, 10 and 30 degrees of freedom compared with the standard normal (black). Small df means heavier tails; with 30 df the t is almost normal."
x_t <- seq(-5, 5, length.out = 400)
t_df <- do.call(rbind, lapply(c(1, 3, 10, 30), \(k) {
  data.frame(x = x_t, density = dt(x_t, df = k), dist = paste0("t, df = ", k))
}))
t_df$dist <- factor(t_df$dist, levels = unique(t_df$dist))

ggplot(t_df, aes(x, density, colour = dist)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 0.9) +
  geom_line(data = data.frame(x = x_t, density = dnorm(x_t)),
            colour = "black", linewidth = 1, linetype = "dashed") +
  labs(x = "x", y = "Density", colour = NULL)
```

- **t** — symmetric like the normal but with heavier tails, because it accounts for the extra uncertainty of estimating $\sigma$ from the data. Used for means: [t-tests](../08-inference/34-t-tests.qmd), confidence intervals for a mean, regression coefficients.

```{r}
#| label: fig-chisq-f
#| fig-cap: "Chi-square (left) and F (right) distributions for a few degrees of freedom. Both take only positive values and are right-skewed."
#| layout-ncol: 2
x_c <- seq(0.05, 20, length.out = 400)
c_df <- do.call(rbind, lapply(c(1, 3, 5, 10), \(k) {
  data.frame(x = x_c, density = dchisq(x_c, df = k), df = factor(k))
}))
ggplot(c_df, aes(x, density, colour = df)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 0.9) +
  coord_cartesian(ylim = c(0, 0.5)) +
  labs(x = "x", y = "Density", colour = "df", title = "Chi-square")

x_f <- seq(0.01, 5, length.out = 400)
f_pars <- list(c(2, 10), c(5, 20), c(10, 50))
f_df <- do.call(rbind, lapply(f_pars, \(d) {
  data.frame(x = x_f, density = df(x_f, d[1], d[2]),
             df = paste0("(", d[1], ", ", d[2], ")"))
}))
ggplot(f_df, aes(x, density, colour = df)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 0.9) +
  labs(x = "x", y = "Density", colour = "df", title = "F")
```

- **Chi-square** ($\chi^2$) — positive and right-skewed; a sum of squared standard normal values. Used for tests on [tables of counts](../08-inference/35-proportions-chisq.qmd).
- **F** — positive and right-skewed, the ratio of two variances, with two df parameters. Used in [ANOVA](../08-inference/37-anova.qmd) and to compare regression models.

They have their own `d/p/q/r` functions: `dt()`, `pt()`, `qt()`, `rt()`; `dchisq()`, `pchisq()`, …; `df()`, `pf()`, … For instance `qt(0.975, df = 10)` = `r round(qt(0.975, 10), 3)` replaces 1.96 when a mean is estimated from 11 observations.

## 8. QQ-plots: does a distribution fit my data?

A histogram with a curve on top is a good first look, but the eye is poor at judging the tails. A **quantile–quantile plot (QQ-plot)** is sharper. The idea:

1. sort the data from smallest to largest;
2. compute where those values *would* be if the data came from a standard normal (the theoretical quantiles, `qnorm(ppoints(n))`);
3. plot one against the other.

If the data are normal, the points lie on a **straight line**. Building one by hand shows there is nothing magic about it:

```{r}
#| label: qq-by-hand
set.seed(4)
x <- rnorm(50, mean = 10, sd = 2)
theoretical <- qnorm(ppoints(length(x)))
head(cbind(theoretical, sample = sort(x)))
```

In practice we use `qqnorm()` + `qqline()` in base R, or `stat_qq()` + `stat_qq_line()` in ggplot2. The *pattern* of departures from the line tells you how the data differ from a normal:

```{r}
#| label: fig-qq-shapes
#| fig-cap: "QQ-plots of 200 simulated values from three distributions. Normal data hug the line; right-skewed data bend upward at the right end; heavy-tailed data bend away from the line at both ends."
set.seed(5)
qq_df <- data.frame(
  value = c(rnorm(200), rexp(200), rt(200, df = 3)),
  shape = rep(c("Normal", "Right-skewed (exponential)",
                "Heavy tails (t, 3 df)"), each = 200)
)
qq_df$shape <- factor(qq_df$shape, levels = unique(qq_df$shape))

ggplot(qq_df, aes(sample = value)) +
  stat_qq(alpha = 0.6) +
  stat_qq_line(colour = "#D55E00", linewidth = 1) +
  facet_wrap(~ shape, scales = "free_y") +
  labs(x = "Theoretical normal quantiles", y = "Sample quantiles")
```

::: {.callout-tip .read-output}
## How to read a QQ-plot

- **Points on the line:** the normal model fits.
- **A curve bending up at the right (a "banana"):** right skew — the largest values are larger than a normal would produce.
- **An S-shape with both ends pulled away from the line:** heavy tails — more extreme values than a normal on both sides.
- **A few wiggles at the very ends** are normal for small samples; focus on systematic patterns.
:::

## 9. Fitting a normal model to penguin body mass

Is penguin body mass normally distributed? Let us first try all penguins together, then each species separately.

```{r}
#| label: fig-mass-hist
#| fig-cap: "Body mass by species: histograms (on the density scale) with a normal curve using each species' own mean and SD."
peng <- penguins[!is.na(penguins$body_mass), ]

curves <- do.call(rbind, lapply(levels(peng$species), \(sp) {
  m <- peng$body_mass[peng$species == sp]
  mass_grid <- seq(2500, 6500, by = 10)
  data.frame(species = sp, body_mass = mass_grid,
             density = dnorm(mass_grid, mean = mean(m), sd = sd(m)))
}))
curves$species <- factor(curves$species, levels = levels(peng$species))

ggplot(peng, aes(body_mass)) +
  geom_histogram(aes(y = after_stat(density)), bins = 20,
                 fill = "grey75", colour = "white") +
  geom_line(data = curves, aes(y = density), colour = "#D55E00",
            linewidth = 1) +
  facet_wrap(~ species, ncol = 1) +
  labs(x = "Body mass (g)", y = "Density")
```

```{r}
#| label: fig-mass-qq
#| fig-cap: "QQ-plots of body mass: all penguins pooled (left) and by species (right)."
#| layout-ncol: 2
ggplot(peng, aes(sample = body_mass)) +
  stat_qq(alpha = 0.5) +
  stat_qq_line(colour = "#D55E00", linewidth = 1) +
  labs(x = "Theoretical quantiles", y = "Body mass (g)", title = "All species")

ggplot(peng, aes(sample = body_mass, colour = species)) +
  stat_qq(alpha = 0.6) +
  stat_qq_line(linewidth = 1) +
  labs(x = "Theoretical quantiles", y = "Body mass (g)",
       title = "By species", colour = NULL)
```

::: {.callout-tip .read-output}
## How to read these plots

- **Pooled**, the points bend away from the line: mixing a heavy species (Gentoo) with two lighter ones produces a right-skewed distribution (mean `r round(mean(peng$body_mass))` g vs median `r round(median(peng$body_mass))` g) that a single normal describes poorly.
- **Within each species** the histograms are close to the normal curves and the QQ-points are close to straight lines. A normal model *per species* is a reasonable simplification.
- The lesson generalises: a variable can be non-normal overall simply because it **mixes groups**. Look for structure before blaming the distribution.
:::

::: {.callout-warning .pitfall}
## Common pitfalls

1. **Treating `dnorm()` as a probability.** For a continuous variable it is a density (it can even exceed 1). Probabilities are areas: use `pnorm()`.
2. **Off-by-one errors with discrete tails.** $P(X \ge 10)$ is `pbinom(9, ...)` with `lower.tail = FALSE`, not `pbinom(10, ...)`.
3. **Passing the variance instead of the SD.** `pnorm(x, mean, sd)` wants the **standard deviation**: `sd = 2`, not `sd = 4`, for a variance of 4.
4. **Mixing up `p` and `q`.** `p*()` takes a value and returns a probability; `q*()` takes a probability and returns a value.
5. **Expecting real data to be exactly normal.** No real variable is. The question is whether the normal is a *useful approximation* for the purpose at hand; QQ-plots help, formal normality tests on large samples flag irrelevant deviations.
:::

## 10. Check your understanding

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" icon="false"}
## Q1. Which distribution would you use for (a) the number of heads in 50 coin tosses, (b) the number of emails you receive in an hour, (c) adult height?

(a) Binomial(50, 0.5): a fixed number of independent trials. (b) Poisson: a count of events in a time interval with no fixed maximum. (c) Approximately normal: the sum of many small genetic and environmental effects.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" icon="false"}
## Q2. What do `pnorm(1.96)` and `qnorm(0.975)` have in common?

They are inverses: `pnorm(1.96)` ≈ 0.975 and `qnorm(0.975)` ≈ 1.96. Since the normal is symmetric, 95% of its area lies between −1.96 and 1.96.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" icon="false"}
## Q3. A QQ-plot shows points that follow the line in the middle but rise steeply above it at the right end. What does this suggest?

Right skew: the largest values are larger than a normal distribution would predict. A log transformation or a method that does not assume normality may be appropriate.
:::

## 11. Exercises

### Interactive (run in your browser)

::: {.exercise}
[★]{.stars} **Exercise 1 — the guessing student.** A quiz has 20 questions with 4 options each. A student guesses every answer. Compute (a) the probability of exactly 5 correct answers, (b) the probability of 10 or more, and (c) check (b) with 10,000 simulated students.

```{webr}
#| exercise: ex_29_1
dbinom(______, size = 20, prob = 0.25)
pbinom(______, size = 20, prob = 0.25, lower.tail = FALSE)

set.seed(1)
sim <- rbinom(10000, size = ______, prob = ______)
mean(sim >= 10)
```

::: {.hint exercise="ex_29_1"}
For "10 or more" use `pbinom(9, ...)` with `lower.tail = FALSE`, because $P(X \ge 10) = 1 - P(X \le 9)$.
:::

::: {.solution exercise="ex_29_1"}
```r
dbinom(5, size = 20, prob = 0.25)                      # about 0.202
pbinom(9, size = 20, prob = 0.25, lower.tail = FALSE)  # about 0.014
set.seed(1)
sim <- rbinom(10000, size = 20, prob = 0.25)
mean(sim >= 10)                                        # close to 0.014
```
Five correct answers is the single most likely result (it is the mean, $20 \times 0.25$). Passing by pure guessing happens to only about 1.4% of students.
:::
:::

::: {.exercise}
[★★]{.stars} **Exercise 2 — normal probabilities and cut-offs.** Scores on a standardised test are approximately $N(100, 15)$. Find (a) the proportion of people scoring above 130, (b) the proportion between 85 and 115, (c) the score needed to be in the top 5%.

```{webr}
#| exercise: ex_29_2
pnorm(______, mean = 100, sd = 15, lower.tail = FALSE)
pnorm(115, mean = 100, sd = 15) - pnorm(______, mean = 100, sd = 15)
q______(0.95, mean = 100, sd = 15)
```

::: {.hint exercise="ex_29_2"}
(b) is an interval: `pnorm(b) - pnorm(a)`. (c) goes from a probability to a value, so it needs `qnorm()`.
:::

::: {.solution exercise="ex_29_2"}
```r
pnorm(130, mean = 100, sd = 15, lower.tail = FALSE)              # about 0.023
pnorm(115, mean = 100, sd = 15) - pnorm(85, mean = 100, sd = 15) # about 0.683
qnorm(0.95, mean = 100, sd = 15)                                 # about 124.7
```
130 is 2 SD above the mean, so about 2.3% score higher (half of the 5% outside ±2 SD). 85–115 is ±1 SD: the familiar 68%.
:::
:::

::: {.exercise}
[★★]{.stars} **Exercise 3 — a call centre.** A call centre receives on average 4 calls every 10 minutes. Using a Poisson model, find the probability of (a) no calls in a 10-minute window and (b) more than 8 calls. (c) Simulate 10,000 windows with `rpois()` and compare the mean and the variance of the counts.

```{webr}
#| exercise: ex_29_3
dpois(______, lambda = 4)
ppois(______, lambda = 4, lower.tail = FALSE)

set.seed(1)
calls <- r______(10000, lambda = 4)
c(mean = mean(calls), var = var(calls))
```

::: {.hint exercise="ex_29_3"}
"More than 8" is $P(X > 8) = 1 - P(X \le 8)$, so the cut-off is 8. The random generator is `rpois()`.
:::

::: {.solution exercise="ex_29_3"}
```r
dpois(0, lambda = 4)                        # about 0.018
ppois(8, lambda = 4, lower.tail = FALSE)    # about 0.021
set.seed(1)
calls <- rpois(10000, lambda = 4)
c(mean = mean(calls), var = var(calls))     # both close to 4
```
Mean and variance are both close to $\lambda = 4$, the signature of a Poisson distribution.
:::
:::

::: {.exercise}
[★★]{.stars} **Exercise 4 — read the QQ-plot.** Draw normal QQ-plots of the built-in `rivers` (lengths of 141 North American rivers) and `faithful$waiting` (waiting times between eruptions of the Old Faithful geyser). Before running, predict which one is right-skewed. What else do you notice?

```{webr}
#| exercise: ex_29_4
par(mfrow = c(1, 2))
qqnorm(______, main = "rivers"); qqline(rivers)
qqnorm(______, main = "faithful$waiting"); qqline(faithful$waiting)
par(mfrow = c(1, 1))
```

::: {.hint exercise="ex_29_4"}
Fill in `rivers` and `faithful$waiting`. Then look at the ends of each plot, and make a `hist()` of each variable if the pattern is unclear.
:::

::: {.solution exercise="ex_29_4"}
```r
par(mfrow = c(1, 2))
qqnorm(rivers, main = "rivers"); qqline(rivers)
qqnorm(faithful$waiting, main = "faithful$waiting"); qqline(faithful$waiting)
par(mfrow = c(1, 1))
```
`rivers` shows the "banana" of strong right skew: a few very long rivers. `faithful$waiting` is not skewed but shows a step (two flat stretches joined by a jump): the data are **bimodal**, with a cluster of short and a cluster of long waits — `hist(faithful$waiting)` confirms it. Neither variable is well described by one normal distribution.
:::
:::

### Practice on your own computer

::: {.exercise}
[★★★]{.stars} **Exercise 5 — checking the 68% rule on real data.** For each penguin species, compute the proportion of birds whose flipper length (`flipper_len`) lies within one standard deviation of the species mean. Compare with the normal value `pnorm(1) - pnorm(-1)` and draw QQ-plots by species. Is the normal model reasonable?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Solution
```r
within_1sd <- function(x) {
  x <- x[!is.na(x)]
  mean(abs(x - mean(x)) < sd(x))
}
tapply(penguins$flipper_len, penguins$species, within_1sd)
pnorm(1) - pnorm(-1)

ggplot(penguins, aes(sample = flipper_len)) +
  stat_qq() +
  stat_qq_line(colour = "#D55E00") +
  facet_wrap(~ species) +
  labs(x = "Theoretical quantiles", y = "Flipper length (mm)")
```
The proportions are roughly 0.71 (Adelie), 0.68 (Chinstrap) and 0.63 (Gentoo), all near 0.68. The QQ-plots are close to straight lines; small "staircase" steps appear because flipper lengths are recorded as whole millimetres. A normal model per species is a reasonable approximation. (ggplot2 drops the rows with missing values with a warning.)
:::
:::

## Summary

| Distribution | Describes | `d` / `p` / `q` / `r` | Mean |
|---|---|---|---|
| Binomial$(n, p)$ | successes in $n$ trials | `dbinom()`, `pbinom()`, `qbinom()`, `rbinom()` | $np$ |
| Poisson$(\lambda)$ | events in an interval | `dpois()`, `ppois()`, `qpois()`, `rpois()` | $\lambda$ |
| Uniform$(a, b)$ | equally likely values | `dunif()`, `punif()`, `qunif()`, `runif()` | $(a+b)/2$ |
| Normal$(\mu, \sigma)$ | sums of many small effects | `dnorm()`, `pnorm()`, `qnorm()`, `rnorm()` | $\mu$ |
| t, $\chi^2$, F | reference distributions for tests | `dt()`/`pt()`/…, `dchisq()`/…, `df()`/… | — |
| QQ-plot | compare data with the normal | `qqnorm()` + `qqline()`, `stat_qq()` + `stat_qq_line()` | — |

- `d` = height/probability of one value, `p` = probability up to a value, `q` = value for a probability, `r` = random draws.
- For continuous variables, **probabilities are areas**; use `lower.tail = FALSE` for upper tails.
- In a normal distribution 68%, 95% and 99.7% of values lie within 1, 2 and 3 SD of the mean; z-scores put everything on the standard scale.
- QQ-plots reveal skew, heavy tails and mixtures far better than histograms; non-normality is often a sign of hidden groups.
